Sow Seeds - Trust The Promise 

by: Gordon Webber 


Between Seasons in 
the Alberta 
Camping Association 

by: Colin E. Lumby, Ph.D. 

The Spring of 1983 saw renewed efforts at pre¬ 
camp preparation of camp staff on a province¬ 
wide basis. 

The advantages of common training courses 
included an interchange of expertise, ideas, 
good fellowship and an identity with the camp¬ 
ing movement as it was represented by the ACA. 

A total of 33 resource persons voluntarily 
gave their time and effort to 120 camp personnel. 
The workshops were regionalized. The single 
day workshop held in the South for junior staff 
enjoyed limited success in spite of a good 
Program Committee headed up by Karen Hirl. 
The single day format did not allow the program 
nor the group processes to really get off the 
ground. The weekend workshops were held on 
consecutive weekends at the beginning of June. 
Yo-Wo-Ch-As Centre, west of Edmonton was 
the scene of the northern workshop which was 
successfully chaired by Rick Matishak. The 
southern event was effectively run by Mike 
Walters operating on his home turf at Yamnuska 
Centre. The sites were perfect and the programs 
while not identical yielded: positive feelings 
about each other; a sharpening of the leader¬ 
ship role and an increased awareness of the 
camp movement in general. In planning for 1984 
Workshops organizers will have to bear in mind 
the successes of 1983 sessions. The extended 
period (48 hrs) allowed special relationships 
and idea sharing to take place. 

At Yo-Wo-Ch-As the most worthwhile offer¬ 
ings included wide games, cooperative games, 
and the survival or animal game. Drama and 
nature oriented activities ranked high. At Yam¬ 
nuska the continuing thread of “generic skills” 
developed during several sessions by Bruce 
Elkin proved to be the most popular. Van Matre’s 
Acclimatization Program "Touch the Earth” as 
well as another session “Communications” 
were highly rated. The programs were varied 
and the Education Committee of Colin Lumby, 
Rea Bryant and Barbara Forster were encour¬ 
aged to formulate plans for 1984. Two regional 
weekend workshops are planned for the first 
weekend in June. 


ASSISTANTSHIPS IN OUTDOOR 
TEACHER EDUCATION 
Northern Illinois University 

Dr. Clifford E. Knapp reports that Graduate 
Teaching Assistantships are available at the 
Taft Field Campus in Outdoor Teacher Educa¬ 
tion at Northern Illinois University for the 1984- 
85 school year beginning in late August. It is 
expected that more than a dozen assistantships 
will be available. 


During September there was a nine day training 
event sponsored by the National Council of 
Churches. It was called the North American 
Church Camp and was held at Epworth Forest 
United Methodist Camp near North Webster, 
Indiana. The theme was “Sow Seeds, Trust The 
Promise" with the introduction of a new curric¬ 
ulum called "Lifestyles of Faithfulness” The 
purpose of the event was to bring representa¬ 
tives from various church camps in North 
America together, present a three year program 
for church camps, and develop training teams 
for each region. 

There are four regions for Canadian church 
camps. Leadership teams from each region are 
responsible for running at least four training 
events in their region. Those involved in church 
camping will most likely be contacted by the 
leadership teams. If, however, you are not con¬ 
tacted or wish to find out more information as 
soon as possible, here are the liaison persons 
for each region: 


These assistantships involve outdoor teaching 
at the Lorado Taft Field Campus, Oregon, IL. 
Because the teaching is primarily with public 
school students and university juniors and 
seniors, priority is given to those applicants who 
have had a minimum of three years experience 
in the elementary or secondary public schools 
or equivalent teaching experience. Graduate 
teaching assistants can earn a Master’s degree 
in outdoor education while meeting assistant-

when groups are in residence. 

Applications and further information may be

ENVIRONMENTAL EDUCATION: 
Notan Endangered Species! 

by: Rick Ireland I I 


Rick Ireland is the Manager of the Edmonton 
YWCA Outdoor Recreation Department which 
operates YoWoChAs, a year-round environmen¬ 
tal and outdoor education centre at Fallis, 
Alberta. 

“It has been just a few years now since the 
words "ecology" and “pollution” have become a 
part of our everyday language. Until recently, 
people just could not see the connection be¬ 
tween the pollution of the environment, the loss 
of eagles and bison and certain wild plants, and 
their own survival. Now, hopefully, they are 
beginning to see that man, the animal, is part of 
the total complex life system on earth; that man, 
too, is one of the endangered species.” 

That statement is from the Alberta Education 
“Environmental Education Manual for Grades 
1-12". The Manual is the result of a two year look 
at the core curriculum of the province’s educa¬ 
tion system and the development of an environ¬ 
mental focus that is compatible with and sup¬ 
portive of the core curriculum. Alberta Education 
is recognizing the need to make students aware 
of their natural environment by teaching a 
respect and an understanding of it. Man (and 
student) has a place in the natural order of 
things and must obey the same laws of nature 
as all other living creatures. Promoting harmony 


through understanding appears to be an integral 
part of the Manual. 

Manuals that provide “how-to” information or 
mini-lesson plans are available to one and all. 
Seldom are they geared to the real, immediate 
needs of the teacher, nor do they present a 
logical, sequential theme for the child’s educa¬ 
tional career. In short, the teacher likely collects 
numerous pieces of information from unrelated 
(and usually foreign) sources and, with some 
hard work, can put a fine environmental program 
together which has deep roots in science and 
social studies. Unfortunately, there is little con¬ 
tinuity from grade to grade and many of the 
remaining subject areas are omitted. 

The Alberta Manual has responded to such 
educational shortcomings with what one might 
call a "package". The core curriculum of each 
grade has been broken down into a number of 
teaching objectives including “knowledge and 
understandings”, “skills, abilities and proces¬ 
ses” and “values and attitudes”. In addition, 
student learning objectives (i.e., what the student 
should be able to do by the end of the section) 
are considered in the areas of physical educa¬ 
tion, language arts, mathematics, science, fine 
arts, health, and social studies. 


To reduce the inevitable confusion that will 
result, all of this is put into a neat and concise 
chart that begins to make sense after a short 
period of time! 

The impact this can have on the sponge-like 
brain of a student is that there now exists a 
logical, linked progression of environmental 
education concepts which are tied directly to 
the child’s grade core curriculum from grade 1 
to grade 12. Ideally, the student will be able to 
receive 12 years of graduated environmental 
education knowledge. 

The impact of such a project on environmen¬ 
tal centres such as YoWoChAs Centre in Alberta 
is that we now have a much clearer view of what 
teachers are looking for when they ask us to 
assist in developing a program for their use at 
our Centre. From a marketing standpoint, we are 
in a position to better understand the teacher’s 
needs and can respond accordingly. 

Although the Manual is in an operational 
review phase, and the overall program is 
optional at most schools, its official or even 
unofficial acceptance will greatly enhance the 
level of environmental education ... at least 
within Alberta.

Volunteer Leaders - Continued from Page 7 

Ont: Liz Greenway, Fred Okada, Dorothy Walter 
Man: Bryan Hill, Miriam Kuropatwa 
Sask: Davd Godwin 

Alta: Jan James. Michael Kenny, Wayne Perkins 
BC: Dave Adair 

Arnie Cohen commented at the end of the 
workshop that he felt as though he had “come 
home" being with camping people again. Even 
though it is a few years since Cohen has been 
actively involved with camps, he still had very 
insightful comments to relate the management 
information to our situations in the camping 
association and our camps. Thanks to the 
leadership of two very special people, we be¬ 
lieve that this event will assist the national 
executive, provincial presidents and vice presi¬ 
dents to improve their leadership performance 
capabilities in the camping associations across 
the country.

SUBSCRIPTION RfiTE SPECIffL!!! 

As we endeavour to continually upgrade our magazine content, we are finding more and more material suitable to Camp Staff. Many counsellors 
are requesting reprints of articles and/or entire issues. We would like to encourage Camp Directors to enter full subscriptions to Canadian Camping 
for their Staff and Senior Staff who are not already members of your provincial camping association. We feel it will be an investment well worth it 
and to this end we would like to offer the following special rate: 

After the first two full-rate subscriptions at $6.00/year, we will offer any additional one-year subscriptions at only $4.00/year. Please act now and 
save! Subscribe your staff to Canadian Camping and receive four issues a year: interviews, editorials, advice column, group dynamics exercises, 
articles and much, much more.. .your staff will thank you, your campers will benefit!
